column4: The source section explicitly connects the root of al-amīn to a mount trusted on the road. This verse contrasts Mecca's protected sanctuary with people being seized around it, sharpening the difference between safe passage and danger; its setting is the city, not transport.

The source section develops al-amīn as dependability and safety on a journey. This verse says the Lord of the House fed Quraysh against hunger and secured them from fear, joining provision and safety in a concrete counter-image to a traveler's fatigue and peril.

The source section's dictionary form balīd describes a horse that falls behind the leaders, and a related sense is weakness in work. This verse tells people to hasten toward forgiveness and a Garden, turning lagging into a specific moral failure to reach the goal.

The source section's dictionary form balīd is a horse trailing the leading horses. This verse describes people who hasten to good deeds and are foremost in them, an especially direct moral counterpart to the lagging mount.

The source section's dictionary form balīd describes falling behind the leaders. This verse says that the people in this passage hastened to good deeds; its own contribution is to portray eagerness in action as a trait of the worshippers it describes.

The source section explicitly cites striving toward the Lord and develops a tiring road. This verse promises guidance to God's paths for those who strive for Him, giving the effort-and-route image a specific divine direction.
The source section's dictionary form al-elyes names a camel carrying every load. This verse says a soul is not charged beyond its capacity, placing a clear limit on the image of bearing loads.

The source section links good work and a load-bearing creature. This verse pairs belief and good deeds with a charge only within a soul's capacity and entry into the Garden, showing both the limit on burden and its favorable outcome.

The source section asks who endures and who gives out in a warrior's charge. This verse tells believers not to weaken in pursuing the enemy, notes that both sides suffer pain, and grounds continued pursuit in hope from God.

The source section's warrior imagery turns on who can hold through battle. This verse measures a small patient force against a much larger enemy, making endurance in combat the explicit condition of the advance.

This neighbor revises 8:65's battle ratio and says God has lightened the burden because He knows the fighters are weak. Its own contribution is that perseverance is measured to human capacity, linking the warrior's load to the source section's carrier imagery.

The source section's dictionary form balīd is a horse that lags behind the leaders. This verse rebukes people for clinging heavily to the earth when called to go forth, a specific image of reluctant weight in a campaign.

Following 9:38's rebuke, this verse warns that refusing to go forth will bring punishment and replacement by another people. Its own contribution is the consequence of lagging when summoned to the campaign.

The source section develops trusted and load-bearing mounts, then asks who can endure the road. This verse commands people to go forth light or heavy and struggle with wealth and selves, directly joining burden, action, and campaign.

The source section includes a lagging horse and a charge that fails to continue. This verse says the reluctant group would have followed had the gain been near and the journey easy, but the distance was too long for them; it explicitly ties resolve to road difficulty.

After 9:42's account of reluctance over a long journey, this verse asks why leave was granted before the truthful and liars were distinguished. Its own contribution is to connect the campaign's failure of resolve with truthfulness, echoing the source section's warrior sense of كذب.

The source section's dictionary form balīd names a horse that falls behind the leaders. This verse says that people who did not really wish to go forth were made to lag behind and told to remain with those who stayed, a specific military instance of the image.

This neighbor explains that the people held back in 9:46 would have brought confusion and discord into the campaign. Its own contribution is to mark the difference between a reliable combat companion and a harmful member of the column.

The source section's lagging mount and weakened warrior meet a direct contrary scene here: those left behind rejoice, dislike striving with their wealth and lives, and tell others not to go out in the heat. Their refusal names the faltering action the image makes perceptible.

Following 9:81's description of those who stayed behind, this verse gives their recompense as little laughter and much weeping. Its own contribution is the consequence of choosing ease over the campaign.

After the campaign in 9:81–82, this verse describes the stay-behinds asking to join a later expedition and being told to remain with those who stayed the first time. Its own contribution is the enduring consequence of having failed to hold to the first call.

The source section includes a warrior who attacks and then does not hold his charge. This verse describes the believers turning their backs at Hunayn after their numbers pleased them and the land felt narrow, a concrete battlefield reversal of the steadfast warrior.
This neighbor to the retreat in 9:25 says God sent tranquility and unseen forces after the flight. Its own contribution is the restoration of resolve after the battle's collapse.

The source section's warrior may fail to sustain an attack. This verse describes fighters losing courage, disputing, and disobeying after seeing what they wanted, a direct case of resolve breaking after initial success.

This neighbor to 3:152 pictures the fighters fleeing uphill without looking back while the Messenger calls them from behind. Its own contribution is the physical retreat on rising ground, joining the source section's difficult path to its image of faltering warriors.

The source section includes denial of the final account and weakness in good work. This verse identifies the denier of the Judgment; the next verses specify the social behavior that makes this denial concrete.

This neighbor explains the denier named in 107:1 through his repelling of the orphan. Its own contribution is a concrete failure of care, answering the source section's contrast between action and giving out.

This neighbor continues the portrait of the denier in 107:1–2 by describing failure even to urge feeding the poor. It directly meets the source section's dictionary sense of weakening even in generosity.

The source section describes a person weakening even in generosity. This verse ends by describing people who withhold even small acts of aid, a specific picture of generosity stopping at its lowest measure.

The source section contrasts work that gives out with a reward that is not cut off. This verse contrasts worldly adornment with enduring good deeds that are better in reward and hope, making the persistence of righteous work explicit.

The source section's dictionary form al-elyes names a camel that bears every load. This verse marks a limit to load-bearing: no bearer carries another soul's burden, and each returns to God individually.

The source section's dictionary form al-elyes is a camel able to carry every load. This verse states that no burden-bearer bears another's burden and then names the return to God, linking load to individual accountability.

The source section's dictionary form al-elyes names a camel carrying all it is loaded with. This verse imagines a heavily burdened soul calling for help, but says none of its load will be carried by another, a precise boundary on the carrier image.

The source section's dictionary form al-elyes describes carrying all loads. This verse repeats that no burden-bearer carries another's burden and connects the limit to the return to God, giving the load image a judgment context.

The source section contrasts a tiring road with an uncut reward. This verse describes people seeking worldly life and its adornment who are repaid for their deeds in this world, a specific near-term payoff distinct from the enduring recompense in the section.

This neighbor completes 11:15's worldly payoff by saying such people have no share in the Hereafter and their deeds come to nothing there. Its own contribution is the boundary between immediate return and lasting reward.

The source section's dictionary form al-elyes names a camel bearing every load. This verse says misleaders will carry their own burdens and added burdens from those they misled, a moral reversal of the reliable load-carrier; its own claim concerns the added burden of leading others astray.
